rewrite.question: A service passed a penetration test six months ago and its code has not changed since. What is the most defensible statement about its security today?
options: It is still secure, because nothing in the code changed
Its dependencies, deployed configuration and threat landscape have moved, so the assessment has aged
It is insecure, because any assessment older than a month is worthless

rewrite.hint: Ask what a penetration test report is a statement about, and what date is on it.
rewrite.explanation: A point-in-time assessment ages even when the code does not: new advisories land against the same dependency versions, base images and platforms accumulate findings, configuration drifts, and attack techniques improve. That is why security is a continuing process with dependency alerts, configuration review and periodic reassessment rather than a milestone you pass. Both extremes are unusable: an unchanged code base is not automatically fine, and a six-month-old report is still evidence, just evidence with a date on it.

rationale: The closing sentiment is true but as written it is guessable from the phrasing alone and carries no engineering content. Grounding it in an aging assessment keeps the objective and makes the learner reason about why security decays without a code change.
